standards.name: MIRAGE Sample Preparation Guidelines (v1.0)
standards.abstract: These guidelines specify minimum reporting for preparation of glycomics samples (carbohydrates, polysaccharides, oligosaccharides and glycoconjugates) derived from biological or chemical starting materials. They cover recording of sample origin (including biologically- or chemically-derived material and descriptions of starting material), sample processing (isolation, enzymatic and chemical modification, and purification) and the designation of the defined final sample. The document (MIRAGE Sample Preparation Guidelines v1.0, 18 Feb 2016) was produced by the MIRAGE initiative/Beilstein-Institut and published in Glycobiology; it aims to improve recording of experimental protocols and reproducibility of glycomics datasets and to provide a common basis for further MIRAGE reporting guidelines.

classification.rationale: The source is organized as prose guidance and a checklist of reporting requirements (section headings and descriptive instructions) rather than a field-level metadata table or a sequence-of-steps DAG. Each item is an instruction to describe or report aspects of sample origin, processing, and naming, so it is best modelled as a set of principles.

principles.principle: Guideline purpose: include all aspects of sample generation, purification and modification and improve reproducibility.
principles.evidence: The sample preparation guidelines are designed to include all aspects of sample generation, purification and modification from biological and/or synthetic material. Fundamentally, the application of MIRAGE sample preparation guidelines will lead to improved recording of experimental protocols and reporting of understandable and reproducible glycomics datasets.

principles.principle: Guidelines serve as a common basis for other MIRAGE reporting guidelines to keep data-analysis requirements short and consistent.
principles.evidence: In addition, these guidelines are considered as a common basis for any further MIRAGE reporting guidelines in order to keep the requirements for data analysis short and consistent.

principles.principle: Describe how the original starting sample material was generated or where it was obtained (general information).
principles.evidence: Describe how original starting sample material was generated or where it was obtained. Descriptions may include but are not limited to material produced in the laboratory (e.g. chemically synthesized), acquired from natural sources (e.g. human tissues) or purchased from a commercial manufacturer. In the case of commercial material, provide vendor and applicable item information. Starting material descriptions are further delineated by biologically or chemically derived material.

principles.principle: For biologically derived material, report recombinant expression/cell type, growth/harvest conditions, any cell modifications, and for tissue-derived material report tissue type, treatments, storage conditions and species.
principles.evidence: Biologically derived material includes recombinantly expressed proteins, cells, etc. as well as whole organisms or tissues. For recombinantly produced material, the cell type (e.g. CHO, HEK, NS0 etc.) and growth/harvest conditions should be specified. Any modifications to cells that influence the characteristics of the starting material (e.g. genetic manipulations) should also be stated. For material isolated from tissues, the tissue type, treatments and/or storage conditions should be reported. The species should also be provided.

principles.principle: For chemically derived (synthetic) material, describe how the material was generated and provide synthesis steps or reference protocols.
principles.evidence: Describe how material was generated. If samples were synthetically derived, provide information detailing synthesis steps or specify where the equivalent reaction protocol is available.

principles.principle: Define the type of starting material that contains the oligosaccharide to be analysed (e.g. glycoprotein, proteoglycan, glycolipid, GPI-anchored, free-oligosaccharides, sugar-nucleotides, synthetically derived material).
principles.evidence: Define the type of starting material used or produced that contains the oligosaccharide to be used/analysed in subsequent experiments. These may include glycoprotein(s), proteoglycan, glycolipid, GPI-anchored, free-oligosaccharides, sugar-nucleotides or synthetically derived material but are not limited to these definitions.

principles.principle: Report sample processing under three subcategories: isolation, modification and purification.
principles.evidence: The sample processing is divided into 1) isolation, 2) modification and 3) purification subcategories. Required information for each is described below.

principles.principle: For isolation steps, describe enzymes used for oligosaccharide removal or modification, specify vendor or (if in-house) expression/purification procedures, indicate whether treatment was in-solution or immobilized and report temperature, duration, volume and enzyme concentration.
principles.evidence: Describe any enzymes used to for the purpose of oligosaccharide removal (e.g. PNGase F) or for modification of the starting material (e.g. trypsin protease). Specify where it was obtained (vendor) or for enzymes produced in-house, describe expression and purification procedure. Also state if sample material was treated in-solution or immobilized (SDS-PAGE, PVDF etc.) as well as temperature, duration, volume, enzyme concentration.

principles.principle: For chemical treatments, define the technique for oligosaccharide release or other chemical modifications and provide reaction conditions (temperature, duration, volume and chemical concentrations).
principles.evidence: Define the technique for oligosaccharide release (hydrazinolysis, β-elimination etc.) or other chemical modifications. Provide details of reaction conditions (temperature, duration, volume and chemical concentrations).

principles.principle: For modifications, document the type of modification (e.g. hydrolysis, tagging, isotopic labelling, permethylation/peracetylation), source of materials and kits, reaction conditions, detailed workflow, and enzyme-specific details (concentration, supplier, biological source). If novel glycosidase used, provide origin (species).
principles.evidence: Describe any treatments made to the isolated material. Explain the type of modification employed (e.g. hydrolysis, sample tagging Chemical modifications (including fluorescent labels), isotopic labelling, permethylation/peracetylation, etc.). Include source of materials, description of kits used, reaction conditions and detailed workflow. Document enzyme concentration, supplier, biological source, incubation time and temperature. If novel glycosidase was used, provide information indicating the origin (i.e. species) of the enzyme.

principles.principle: For purification steps, specify all purification steps used after isolation/modification and, for each method, describe experimental materials and methods (e.g. stationary phase, flow rates, fractionation).
principles.evidence: Specify all steps used to purify starting material after isolation/modification steps. Examples of procedures include solid phase extraction (SPE), liquid-liquid extraction or other chromatographic methods. For each method describe the all experimental materials (e.g. stationary phase) and methods (e.g. flow rates, fractionation etc.).

principles.principle: Provide a designation/name for the final sample in accordance with conventional nomenclature and specify the sample type to be analysed.
principles.evidence:
Provide a designation for the final sample in accordance with conventional terminology. Resources for glycoconjugate and oligosaccharide nomenclature are available in Essentials of Glycobiology (Varki, A., Cummins, R., et al. 2009) and Essentials of Carbohydrate Chemistry and Biochemistry (Lindhorst, T.K. 2003).

Name or specify the type of sample material to be analysed or used in other experiments. These may include but are not limited to glycoconjugates, glycosaminoglycans, N- or O-glycans, glycopeptides, glycolipids, monosaccharides, poly- and oligosaccharides.

standards.notes: Source: MIRAGE Sample Preparation Guidelines Version 1.0 (18 Feb 2016), doi:10.3762/mirage.1; published in Glycobiology 2016, 26(9):907-910. Extracted from PDF 'MIRAGE Sample Preparation Guidelines'.

standards.name: MIRAGE Mass Spectrometric (MS) Analysis Guidelines for Glycans and Glycoproteins (v1.0)
standards.abstract: These guidelines describe metadata to report mass-spectrometric analyses of glycans and glycoproteins. The research objects are mass spectra and derived structural/analytical data for glycans and glycoproteins acquired under diverse ionisation and mass analyser conditions (ESI, MALDI, TOF, ion traps, ion mobility, etc.). The document is MIRAGE MS Guidelines v1.0 (April 24, 2013), based on the MIAPE-MS template, prepared by the MIRAGE working group (Beilstein-Institut and community contributors) to standardize what information (instrument, acquisition parameters, source details, post-source componentry and processing/analysis software) should be reported to ensure interpretability and reproducibility of glycomics MS data.

classification.rationale: The source presents a template/checklist of named metadata fields with expected formats and examples (e.g. "Date stamp ... 'YYYY-MM-DD' format"), not prose instructions. Each entry names a specific field and in many cases gives a concrete data format or controlled vocabulary, so the material is a metadata table.

standards.name: MIRAGE Glycan Microarray Guidelines (v1.0)
standards.abstract: These guidelines cover reporting of glycan microarray experiments—assays that measure binding between a Glycan Binding Sample (proteins, cells, viruses, aptamers, etc.) and arrays composed of defined or undefined glycans printed onto solid supports and scanned to produce image and numerical data. The MIRAGE Glycan Microarray Guidelines (Version 1.0, 22 June 2016) were produced by the MIRAGE project/Commission (published DOI:10.3762/mirage.3) to define minimal, intentionally succinct reporting requirements for generating interpretable glycan microarray data, and provide templates and exemplar documents to help researchers include essential sample, array, printing, detection, data-processing and interpretation information. The scope addresses reporting items required to unambiguously describe array content, sample preparation and assay/processing parameters; it was drafted to be minimal and applicable across different platforms while encouraging retention of raw and intermediate data.

classification.rationale: The source is organized as prose guidelines and a reporting template that list required information to report (instructions and headings) rather than a fully typed field-level metadata table. The document enumerates eight workflow areas and gives narrative descriptions of the minimal information to include for each, i.e. guidance/checklist items (principles), not concrete data type definitions.

principles.principle: Overall scope — eight workflow areas and three data levels
principles.evidence:
We have identified 8 areas, numbered in the workflow shown below, that are required for generating an unambiguous glycan array in the first instance and obtaining binding data. For each numbered component of the workflow area we provide guidelines for the minimal information that should be provided in reporting results.

Similar to DNA microarray experiment, there are three levels of data relevant to a glycan microarray experiment:
Level 1: Raw data (original TIFF image from array scanner)
Level 2: Quantified numerical data output file (e.g. proscan or gpr) from scanner software
Level 3: Processed data (after association with glycan identities, averaging of replicates with appropriate statistics, data selection procedures, filtering and sorting, etc.)
The present MIRAGE guidelines suggest that only ‘Level 3’ data need be presented in published papers but also suggest that ‘Level 1’ and ‘Level 2’ data be retained by researchers so that it be available when suitable databases and processing software become accessible and that deeper data comparison and mining can be undertaken where worthwhile.

principles.principle: Sample (Glycan Binding Sample) — report identification, origin and preparation
principles.evidence:
The Sample description should include an appropriate name, previous references, public database IDs (if available), its origin (synthetic, natural, or recombinant), and its source including vendor or method of preparation.
For organisms, the protocol for propagation should be included.
Description of Sample
For proteins, a statement of purity is required and may represent a quantitative or qualitative description; i.e., % purity based on a specific assay (quantitative) or a component of a mixture such as a polyclonal antibody in a serum sample (qualitative). Fusion constructs for recombinant proteins for the purpose of detecting should also be described.

principles.principle: Sample modifications and labelling — describe any labels and modification methods
principles.evidence:
If sample is directly labelled, describe the method and reagents
Sample modifications (including sources) used for chemical labeling of the Sample, e.g. fluorescein, biotin, etc.

principles.principle: Assay protocol — report concentrations, buffers, blocking, incubation and washing conditions, and secondary reagents
principles.evidence: The protocol used for microarray binding analysis of Sample should include Sample concentration. Describe the composition of solutions, time and temperature used for blocking (preventing non-specific binding) binding, and washing, as well as application of secondary reagent(s) required for the analyses. If the Sample is precomplexed with secondary detection reagents prior to adding to the array (e.g. anti-His antibody with his-tagged Sample) give the ratio of reactants and pre-complexing time and temperature.

principles.principle: Glycan library — report glycan identity, structure, registry/accession where possible, source and purity
principles.evidence:
Glycan arrays may be comprised of monosaccharides, oligosaccharides, polysaccharides or other glycoconjugates (glycolipids or glycoproteins)... Regardless of type, the glycan array is generated from a glycan library. ... For mono- and oligosaccharides, the structure of each glycan, i.e. the sequence, linkage and anomeric configuration of each Glycan description for defined monosaccharide should be indicated using an appropriate nomenclature, which may be textual or symbolic as in SNFG (doi: 10.1093/glycob/cwv091).
When possible, accession numbers assigned by an authoritative informatics resource, such as the GlyTouCan glycan structure registry (https://glytoucan.org/) should be included. ... The purity of each glycan should be indicated [MIRAGE Sample Preparations Guidelines (doi:10.3762/mirage.1) are recommended]. Sources/references of glycans should be specified.

principles.principle: Glycan modifications and derivatization — document methods and linker structures and indicate effects on structure and purity
principles.evidence: Methods/references for functionalization or derivatization of glycans, including the structures of linkers should be described. Any effects on the glycan structure; i.e., reductive amination of reducing monosaccharide, should be indicated. The purity of each glycan derivative should be indicated.

principles.principle: Printing surface — describe substrate type, manufacturer and any custom preparation and immobilization chemistry
principles.evidence:
What type of surface is being used; i.e., microscope-glass slide, microtiter plate or other format.
Manufacturers of coated microscope slides, microtiter plates or other types of surfaces will provide a general description of their product. Provide the name of the manufacturer or name provided by the vendor with appropriate description of the product. If the slides were custom prepared/coated, indicate the initial source and description of the starting surface; i.e., glass material, microtiter plate, etc., and the protocol used to prepare the surface prior to sample deposition.
Describe the non-covalent immobilization method; e.g. adsorption of lipid-linked glycans to nitrocellulose, or neoglycoprotein conjugates to polystyrene, nitrocellulose, etc.
Describe the chemistry on the slide surface that enables the covalent immobilization of the glycan samples; e.g. NHS-ester or epoxide for amine functional groups, maleimide for sulfhydryl functional group.

principles.evidence:
4. Arrayer (Printer)

(Template headings listing required items): Description of Arrayer; Dispensing mechanism; Glycan deposition; Printing conditions

principles.evidence:

principles.principle: Detector, scanning and image analysis — report scanner hardware, settings and image-analysis software and data processing steps
principles.evidence:
6. Detector and Data Processing
Scanning hardware GenePix 4300A (Molecular Devices, UK)
Scanning resolution: 10 μm / pixel
Laser channel: Red (scan wavelength 635 nm)
Scanner PMT: 350
Image analysis GenePix® Pro 7 (Molecular Devices)
Data processing
The gpr files were entered into an in-house microarray database using software ... for data processing. No particular Data normalization method or statistical analysis was used for the results of the screening arrays.

principles.principle: Data presentation — specify which processed data (Level 3) are presented and where results/figures/tables are provided
principles.evidence:
The present MIRAGE guidelines suggest that only ‘Level 3’ data need be presented in published papers but also suggest that ‘Level 1’ and ‘Level 2’ data be retained by researchers ...
7. Glycan Microarray Data Presentation
The microarray binding results are in Figure 2, and Supplementary Table 2.

principles.principle: Data interpretation and conclusions — report methods used for interpretation (or state none) and the conclusions drawn from the microarray data
principles.evidence:
8. Interpretation and Conclusion from Microarray Data
Data interpretation
No software or algorithms were used to interpret processed data.
Conclusions
At the assay condition used, the recombinant CMA1 lectin showed binding showed a broad range of binding activities and bound four types of glycan sequences: galactose (Gal)-terminating, GalNAc-terminating, fucose (Fuc)-terminating and chondroitin sulphate (CS) related sequences.

standards.notes: Extraction focused on the narrative guidelines (principles) in the MIRAGE Glycan Microarray Guidelines v1.0 and the provided template/examples. The source includes an accompanying template (Supplementary Glycan Microarray Information Template) and example supplementary documents that show how the principles are used in practice.

standards.name: MIRAGE Liquid Chromatography Analysis Guidelines (v1.0)
standards.abstract: These guidelines describe minimal information to report for liquid chromatography (LC) experiments used in glycomics, including instrument configuration, column and mobile phase characteristics, chromatographic run parameters, detection settings, fraction collection and data annotation. The document is MIRAGE's LC reporting guideline (Version 1.0, 1 March 2018; doi:10.3762/mirage.4) and is intended to improve reproducibility and data utility by specifying what metadata should accompany LC-derived chromatographic traces, retention indices, fraction descriptions, and supporting treatments such as exoglycosidase digestion. The scope covers general descriptors, equipment and column details, mobile phase and run properties, pre-/post-run processes, detection and output formats, data annotation and exoglycosidase treatment reporting.

classification.rationale: The source is a prose guidelines document listing items that should be reported (instructions/checklist style). It enumerates reporting requirements rather than presenting a typed metadata table or a sequential workflow, so it fits the 'principle' classification.

principles.principle: Responsible person or institution (contact and identifiers)
principles.evidence: Responsible person or The primary contact person for this data set; this could be the experimentalist, principal investigator etc. Provide affiliation and contact supporting information including Department, Institution, Email and Phone number (not compulsory). Additional persistent digital identifiers e.g. ORCID can be used.

principles.principle: Time stamp (date and time of LC experiment)
principles.evidence: Time stamp Date and time the LC experiment was performed (start time).

principles.principle: Sample preparation provenance and parameters
principles.evidence: Sample Preparation Any general and specific parameters, settings, conditions important for tracing the sample preparation history as outlined in the sample preparation guidelines. standards.name: MIRAGE NMR Glycan Recognition Guidelines (v1.0)
standards.abstract: These guidelines cover reporting of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) experiments used to characterize glycan recognition by receptors (e.g., lectins, antibodies, cells, synthetic glycan-binding molecules). The data modality is NMR spectral and derived data (1H, 13C, 15N chemical shifts; NOEs; J couplings; relaxation times; RDCs/PCSs/PREs; STD intensities) together with experimental parameters and sample descriptions. Published by the MIRAGE initiative (Version 1.0, 21 September 2020, doi:10.3762/mirage.5), the document provides a structured template for what to report as supplementary material: sample composition and quality, spectrometer and experiment parameters, specific NMR observables to report, data presentation, and interpretation/conclusions.

standards.name: MIRAGE Capillary Electrophoresis Guidelines (v1.0)
standards.abstract: These guidelines cover reporting for capillary electrophoresis (CE) experiments applied to glycomics and glycoproteomics, including instrument-based separation (e.g. xCGE-LIF) and generated data files (.ab1 / .fsa) and derived "N-glycan fingerprints". The MIRAGE CE Guidelines (version 1.0) were published by the MIRAGE initiative and the listed authors in Glycobiology; they define a set of metadata items and formats to ensure reproducible reporting of CE experiments (general features, sample and sample-solution composition, instrumentation, analysis type, run processes and step descriptors). The standard addresses what to report (who/when/what was measured and how) for CE-based glycoanalysis so results can be interpreted and compared across studies.

classification.rationale: The source presents named metadata items with specific expected content or formats (e.g. 'Date stamp' with 'YYYY-MM-DD', contact info fields, capillary dimensions, CE mode examples), i.e. a field-level metadata checklist with concrete types/values rather than only prose guidance or procedural steps.

standards.name: MIRAGE Lectin Microarray Analysis Guidelines (v1.0)
standards.abstract: This standard covers reporting of lectin microarray experiments that profile glycan-containing samples (e.g., glycan, glycoprotein, cell lysate, cells, glycopeptides) using lectin microarrays. The data modality is fluorescence microarray scans and derived spot intensity matrices, with associated metadata about samples, lectin library, array production, detector settings, image analysis, and downstream data processing and presentation. The materials provided are a Supplementary Lectin Microarray Document and a Supplementary Lectin Microarray Information Template derived from the MIRAGE guidelines (doi:10.3763/mirage.8). The package is intended as a reporting template/checklist maintained under the MIRAGE initiative to ensure consistent, comprehensive metadata for lectin microarray experiments, covering sample description and preparation, lectin library composition, immobilization surface and array production, detector and image analysis, data processing/statistics, visualization, and data deposition.

classification.rationale: The source material is presented as a fillable metadata template / checklist with named fields (headers) that map to discrete metadata items (e.g., 'Sample', 'Immobilization surface', 'Instrument (scanner, flow cytometer)', etc.). These are concrete field names intended to be completed per experiment (the Supplementary Information template and Example files), so the source's structure is a metadata table rather than prose principles or a workflow DAG.

Assay_protocol.evidence: Assay protocol		After dilution with probing buffer at 0.5 μg/ml, the Cy3-labeled hydrophobic fraction was applied to the lectin microarray and incubated at 20 °C overnight. After washing with probing buffer, fluorescence images were acquired using an evanescent field-activated fluorescence scanner (GlycoStationTM reader 1200; GP BioSciences). The fluorescence signal of each spot was quantified using Array Pro Analyzer version 4.5 (Media Cybernetics, Bethesda, MD), and the background value was subtracted. The background value was obtained from the area without lectin immobilization. The lectin signals of triplicate spots were averaged and normalized to the mean value of 96 lectins immobilized on the array.

Printing_conditions.name: Printing conditions
Printing_conditions.descr: Conditions for spotting and post-spotting processing (concentration, buffer, incubation, blocking).
Printing_conditions.evidence: Printing conditions		Lectins were dissolved at a concentration of 0.5 mg/ml in a spotting solution (Matsunami Glass), and spotted onto epoxysilane-coated glass slides (Schott) in triplicate using a non-contact microarray printing robot (MicroSys4000, Genomic Solutions). The glass slides were then incubated at 25 °C overnight to allow lectin immobilization. The lectin-immobilized glass slides were then washed with probing buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 140 mM NaCl (TBS) containing 2.7 mM KCl, 1 mM CaCl2, 1 mM MnCl2, and 1% Triton X-100) and incubated with blocking reagent N102 (NOF Co.) at 20 °C for 1 h. Finally, the lectin-immobilized glass slides were washed with TBS containing 0.02% NaN3 and stored at 4 °C until use.
